source: Russell and Wefald (1989) On Optimal Game-Tree Search using Rational Meta-Reasoning (IJCAI-89; experimental precursor of the 1991 work)
finding: First real test of 'a thought is an action with cost and value'. MGSS* expands the leaf with the highest estimated search value minus a time cost, and stops when no leaf has positive net value. It played Othello against fixed-depth alpha-beta with the same evaluation function. It won with far fewer nodes, but used MORE wall-clock time at depths 2 and 3 and only slightly less at depth 4, because the metalevel bookkeeping was costly. Against depth-6 alpha-beta it could not build big enough trees and played poorly.
numbers: Each tournament: 32 games from 16 random start positions, colours alternated; depth 2 had one tied game. Roughly even with depth-2 alpha-beta (slightly more nodes), significantly better at depths 3 and 4 with far fewer nodes. Slightly better than even against depth-5 alpha-beta using about 1/6 of the nodes. Time cost tuned per depth so MGSS* generated about as many nodes as alpha-beta at depth 2. Per-tournament win counts and the time column of Table 1 could not be read (garbled PDF text).
quote: the single-step assumption eventually begins to bar almost all nodes from being expanded as the tree grows larger
limits: Only the 1989 conference version was readable. The 1991 Artificial Intelligence paper returned 403 and was not opened. Othello only, one evaluation function, authors' own test, no independent replication found. Node count is not time: the metalevel was slower per node. The weakness at depth 6 is an early sign of the one-step (myopic) failure that Hay 2012 later formalised.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 in part, gap 4 in part. The founding result is node savings with a real overhead cost, and a documented breakdown of the one-step rule when the search gets large. For our gate: count the cost of the gate itself, and do not trust a one-step rule on long chains.

finding: Improved version of the Russell-Wefald algorithm. Tested in Othello against alpha-beta of depth 2 and 6 with the same evaluation function. The time-cost function was tuned at each depth so the algorithm played at least as well as alpha-beta. The author reports a significant improvement over the original MGSS* and a distinct advantage over alpha-beta, roughly 60:1 at depth 6.
numbers: Only the text sentence was readable: 'roughly 60:1 at depth 6'. The results table did not extract from the PDF, so the unit of the 60:1 ratio (nodes, time or games) is not verified by me. Random start positions, colours alternated.
quote: preliminary results show a significant improvement over the original MGSS* algorithm
limits: Author calls the results preliminary. Cost function tuned per opponent depth, a free parameter. Unit of the 60:1 figure unstated in readable text.
agent_relevance: The cost-of-compute parameter had to be tuned per setting to get the savings. A prompt gate will need the same tuning per task type.

source: Xu, Xie, Zhao, He (2025) Chain of Draft: Thinking Faster by Writing Less
finding: A prompt-only change, no training, on closed APIs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet): ask for a five-word-per-step draft instead of full chain of thought. Large token cut, small accuracy cost on the harder item (GSM8K), none on easy items. It is a fixed style, not an item-by-item gate.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT 95.4 (GPT-4o) and 95.8 (Claude) vs CoD 91.1 and 91.4; CoD about 40 tokens per answer, about 80% fewer output tokens, latency cut 76.2% and 48.4%. Coin flip (250 synthetic items): CoT and CoD both 100% for both models, tokens down 68% (GPT-4o) and 86% (Claude). Sports understanding, Claude: tokens 189.4 to 14.3 (92.4% fewer). Date understanding: GPT-4o CoT 90.2 vs CoD 88.1; Claude CoT 87.0 vs CoD 89.7. Zero-shot CoD: Claude gain over direct answer only 3.6 points. Models under 3B: CoD gap to CoT much larger.
quote: reducing the average output token count by 80%
limits: Needs hand-written few-shot drafts; weak zero-shot and on small models. Baseline is few-shot CoT of non-reasoning models, not reasoning models. Authors' own runs, no independent replication seen. Loses 4 points on GSM8K, so not 'equal accuracy' there.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a prompt-only method reaches 68-92% token savings at equal accuracy on easy or symbolic items on closed models. But it is a fixed style, not a per-item gate, and needs few-shot examples.

source: Han, Wang, Fang, Zhao, Ma, Chen (2024; v6 2026) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (TALE)
finding: The closest thing to a prompt-only per-item gate with its own cost counted. TALE-EP asks the same model (GPT-4o-mini) to estimate a token budget for each question, then puts that budget in the prompt. Expense includes the input and output tokens of the estimator call. Big savings on easy items, a real accuracy loss on harder ones.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Table 3 (vanilla CoT -> TALE-EP; accuracy / output tokens / expense in 1e-5 dollars): GSM8K 81.35 / 318 / 541 -> 84.46 / 77 / 280. GSM8K-Zero (easy) 99.50 / 253 / 887 -> 98.72 / 23 / 276. MathBench-Arithmetic 75.00 / 314 / 79 -> 73.67 / 40 / 19. MathBench-Middle 84.67 / 554 / 68 -> 79.33 / 238 / 43. MathBench-High 84.00 / 653 / 82 -> 80.00 / 255 / 48. MathBench-College 78.00 / 676 / 82 -> 70.00 / 260 / 46. Average of 6 sets: accuracy 83.75 -> 81.03, output tokens 461 -> 149 (68.6% fewer), expense 290 -> 118 (59% lower). Direct answering averaged only 52.31%.
quote: reduces token costs by 68.64% on average
limits: Maths only. Accuracy drop grows with difficulty (about -1 on easy, -8 on College). The estimator is the same model. The expense column mixes in input and cached tokens, so a 91% cut in output tokens on GSM8K-Zero becomes a 69% cut in cost. Models often ignore tight budgets and run longer (the authors' 'token elasticity').
agent_relevance: Closes gap 1 (30%+ savings at equal accuracy on easy items, closed API, no training) and gap 2 in cost terms: net of the estimator call, savings fall from 91% of output tokens to 69% of cost on easy items, and to about 44% on College. Accuracy at matched total tokens was not reported.

source: Han et al. (2024; v6 2026) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning, Table 5 (post-trained TALE-PT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct)
finding: Ordinary-benchmark evidence of negative value of computation on easy items: for Llama-3.1-8B, long chain of thought scores below direct answering on GSM8K-Zero, and a budget-trained model beats both.
numbers: GSM8K-Zero: direct 70.32% (13.5 tokens); vanilla CoT 65.04% (251 tokens); TALE-PT-SFT 78.43% (77.9 tokens); TALE-PT-DPO 78.41% (113.4 tokens). GSM8K: direct 21.00%, CoT 77.56% (241.5 tokens), SFT 78.57% (139.6), DPO 74.11% (149.9).
limits: One 8B model. GSM8K-Zero is built so that the answer is implied in the question. Trained, not prompt-only. Note that for GPT-4o-mini the same set shows CoT 99.50 vs direct 97.21, so the sign is model-specific.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 base-rate point: negative VOC appears on a standard easy set, not only on adversarial tasks, but only for a small model and easy items.

source: Paglieri, Cupial, Cook, Piterbarg, Tuyls, Grefenstette, Foerster, Parker-Holder, Rocktaeschel (2026 v3) Learning When to Plan: Efficiently Allocating Test-Time Compute for LLM Agents
finding: Re-read of the paper behind earlier line c19. Zero-shot, planning every k steps gives a non-monotonic 'Goldilocks' curve. The authors tried to get a PROMPTED adaptive planner ('plan only when necessary') and it failed, so no prompt-only dynamic baseline exists. Only SFT then RL gave a working dynamic planner.
numbers: Zero-shot Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, 100 seeds each in POGS and Crafter, k in {1,2,4,8,...} plus never-plan. Performance peaks at intermediate k in both. Trend repeated with Gemini 2.5 Flash and in TextWorld (appendix C.5). Always-plan agent had the highest backtracking rate in POGS. Trained 8B (SFT+RL) beat a Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct baseline with 85% fewer tokens (as in c19). SFT priming was needed: Base+RL plan-dynamically did worse than Base+RL no-plan.
quote: Models struggled to consistently interpret abstract instructions such as 'plan only when necessary'
limits: Games only (Crafter, POGS, TextWorld), Llama and Gemini. No plan-on-surprise rule was run at equal tokens against fixed k; the only dynamic planner is trained, so gap 6 stays open on that comparison.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 6: asking an LLM in plain words to plan only when needed does not work; it falls back to always or never. A hard-coded trigger (surprise, error, new tool output) is the untested alternative.

source: Xiong, Hu, Lu, Li, Fu, He, Hooi (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Closest head-to-head of black-box confidence signals: verbalised confidence vs agreement across samples vs white-box methods, on 5 LLMs (incl. GPT-4, GPT-3.5) and 8 datasets. Verbalised confidence is overconfident and barely predicts errors. Agreement across 5 samples predicts errors far better, most on arithmetic. White-box is only a little better.
numbers: GPT-4 verbalised confidence: average AUROC 62.7% (random is 50%). GSM8K: AUROC 54.8% with verbalised confidence vs 92.7% with 5-sample consistency. GPT-4 on GSM8K at 93.6% accuracy gets low ECE (0.064) by saying 100% every time, but then AUROC is near chance. White-box vs best black-box gap is narrow (0.522 to 0.605 AUROC in the abstract). Gains from more samples flatten between M = 1 and 13. No method wins everywhere; all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
quote: none of these techniques consistently outperform others
limits: Measures failure prediction, not token savings or stopping. 2023-era models, no reasoning models. Consistency costs M times the tokens, so it pays only if stopping saves more than M calls.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for a closed-API agent verbalised confidence is close to useless as a stop signal; sample agreement is the stronger black-box signal.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses token-probability confidence (white-box) of reasoning traces to stop weak traces early in parallel sampling, no training. Large token cuts against full majority voting; the aggressive setting costs accuracy in some cells, and filtering fails when the model is confidently wrong.
numbers: Budget 512 traces. Against majority voting (cons@512): DeepConf-low cuts tokens 43-79% (up to 84.7% in the abstract), DeepConf-high 18-59%. DeepSeek-8B means: low 62.88% fewer tokens, high 47.67%. Example (tokens x1e8, accuracy): DeepSeek-8B AIME24 cons 3.55 / 86.7 -> low 0.78 (-77.9%) / 92.5. Qwen3-32B BRUMO25: low is -0.9 accuracy. GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25: cons 92.8, low 92.0. Filtering to the top 10% can hurt through overconfidence on wrong answers (GPT-OSS-120B); a 90% filter is safer. GPT-OSS-120B reaches 99.9% on AIME25.
limits: Baseline is 512-sample voting, a very expensive reference, not a single answer. Needs log-probabilities, which not all closed APIs give. Maths only. Threshold is set from a warm-up set of traces, which costs tokens too.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: logprob confidence works as a stop signal but fails when the model is confidently wrong; same failure as verbalised confidence, smaller.

source: Yang, Si, Duan et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free. At 'Wait'-like switch points the model is prompted for a trial answer; if the trial answer has high token confidence, thinking stops. Across 11 reasoning models and 10 benchmarks it shortens chains and slightly raises accuracy. The appendix shows switch words sit at high-entropy positions where the hidden state changes most, so uncertainty is visible in the text.
numbers: Average chain length down 19.1% to 80.1% across the 11 models, accuracy up 0.3 to 5.0 points. Latency down 27.9% for the original and 36.3-58.6% for a faster variant. Cosine similarity of hidden states is lower at marker words than at normal tokens (Table 11).
quote: reducing the length of CoT sequences by an average of 19.1% to 80.1% while improving accuracy by 0.3% to 5.0%
limits: Ranges across models, not uniform. Two other papers find DEER hurts on some sets (d10, d11). Open-weight reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a switch signal visible in the text ('Wait', 'Alternatively') is a cheap trigger for a probe. Our S6 trigger could be a surface marker rather than a hidden-state probe.

source: Li, Qin, Wang et al. (2026) Stop When Further Reasoning Won't Help: Attention-State Adaptive Generation (ASAG)
finding: The one head-to-head found that puts prompt-based, answer-agreement, confidence and attention signals in one table on the same models and benchmarks. Differences between adaptive signals are small; the large gap is between no-thinking and the rest.
numbers: Average accuracy / compression ratio (length vs vanilla, lower is shorter) over 5 benchmarks. Qwen3-4B: vanilla 71.0; NoThinking 54.8 / 34.3%; TALE (prompt budget) 67.1 / 58.7%; Dynasor (answer agreement across probes) 71.6 / 64.4%; DEER (confidence) 71.3 / 64.4%; ASAG (attention) 73.9 / 63.5%. Qwen3-8B: vanilla 72.5; NoThinking 59.8 / 40.3%; TALE 70.5 / 68.9%; Dynasor 72.8 / 69.7%; DEER 73.4 / 63.5%; ASAG 75.1 / 64.2%. So adaptive signals keep roughly a third of the tokens off at about equal accuracy and differ by 1-3 points. DEER drops sharply on some cells of the other blocks (rows partly interleaved in the PDF text).
limits: One preprint by the proposing group, so ASAG is favoured. Only the average columns of the 4B and 8B blocks were read cleanly. Open-weight models, maths and GPQA. Compression is about 35%, below the 60-80% in other papers.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 in part: no signal is clearly best; a prompt budget (TALE) loses 2-4 points on reasoning models; agreement and confidence are about equal; skipping thinking costs 12-17 points here.

source: Sun, Cheng, Li, Chen, Wang (2025) Stop When Enough: Adaptive Early-Stopping for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning (REFRAIN)
finding: Training-free stop rule: detect reflective-but-redundant steps with a two-stage discriminator and set the stop threshold with a bandit controller. A second independent comparison against DEER and Deepconf, with a different ranking from d10.
numbers: Qwen3-8B vs vanilla thinking: GSM8K +0.30 accuracy with 35.9% fewer tokens; MATH-500 -0.20 with 39.0% fewer; CSQA +0.90 with 54.2% fewer; GPQA-Diamond +6.56 with 21.5% fewer. The text says DEER saves tokens but 'performs noticeably worse than Vanilla on GSM8K and MATH-500' with Qwen3. Abstract: 20-55% token cut across four benchmarks and two model families.
limits: Table row labels did not extract reliably; numbers above are taken from the text and the REFRAIN row. Proposing group's own comparison. Qwen3-8B and gpt-oss only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: rankings of stop signals flip between papers (DEER fine in d10, hurt here), so none has a robust edge. Any gate must be validated on our own tasks.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models (ICML 2025)
finding: Large-scale measure of how often different LLMs make the same mistake. Errors are strongly correlated, more so for bigger and more accurate models, even across providers.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions (HuggingFace leaderboard); 71 LLMs on 14,042 questions (HELM); 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume-job pairs. On HELM, model pairs pick the same wrong answer about 60% of the time when both err; random choice among wrong options would give 1/3. Same provider, same architecture and similar size raise agreement; higher accuracy raises it too after those controls.
quote: models agree 60% of the time when both models err
limits: Cross-model, not repeated samples from one model; multiple choice only. Same-model samples are probably MORE correlated than cross-model pairs, but this was not measured. No calibration of Adaptive-Consistency's independence assumption.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, partly: independence between models is false and gets worse for strong models. Treat agreement as a floor on risk, not a probability.

source: Chen, Davis, Hooi, Zou, Zhang et al. (2024) Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards Scaling Laws of Compound Inference Systems
finding: Majority-vote accuracy can first rise and then FALL as the number of calls grows, because on hard queries the wrong answer is the likelier one and voting amplifies it. A mix of easy and hard queries gives a non-monotone curve and an optimal number of calls.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read only; no cell values recorded. Theory plus experiments on several language tasks; the scaling model predicts the best number of calls from a small sample.
limits: Abstract and introduction only. Plain majority vote, not adaptive stopping. Assumes samples independent given the query.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 9: on a query that is hard for the model, more samples plus stop-on-agreement makes the wrong answer look settled. A stop rule needs a difficulty guard or a check that the modal answer beats chance.

source: Oladri, Jawahar, Mohamed (2026) Token Budget Saturation and Mechanistic Early-Detection of Reasoning Non-Convergence in Chain-of-Thought Models
finding: A per-item rule before the answer exists is weak. On a 7B distilled reasoning model, whether a chain converges is only slightly predicted by item difficulty, and a hidden-state probe at token 150 is barely above chance. Non-converging chains are mostly wrong.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 1983-2024. GSM8K and MATH-500 reach 95% of uncapped accuracy at 256 thinking tokens. AIME: 56.5% of generations converge with 96.5% accuracy; 43.5% never terminate by 10,000 tokens and get 11.5% accuracy. Difficulty explains little of convergence (r squared 0.186). Best probe: layer 20 at token 150, AUC 0.608 +- 0.080; probes beat behavioural baselines at 8 of 9 checkpoints by mean AUC +0.035, but n = 200 is too small to confirm. AIME 2025 check: converged 100% accuracy, non-converged 0%.
limits: One small distilled model, maths only, n = 200 for probes, preprint under review. High accuracy of converged chains may partly reflect memorised older AIME items (the 2025 check argues against it).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: no cheap per-item rule exists. Item difficulty barely predicts who overthinks. The usable signal is in-run: a chain that has not converged by a token cap is very likely wrong, so cap and switch strategy rather than predict.

source: Shojaee, Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Horton, Bengio, Farajtabar (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On controlled puzzles, at equal token budgets, plain models match or beat their thinking versions on easy items, thinking wins at medium difficulty, and both collapse at high difficulty. Reasoning effort even falls near the collapse point.
numbers: Pairs: Claude 3.7 Sonnet with and without thinking; DeepSeek R1 vs V3; QwQ-32B vs Qwen2.5-32B in the appendix. Complexity varied by problem size N. Three regimes as described. Exact accuracies sit in figures that were not read.
limits: Constructed puzzles, exactly the kind of task a base-rate study should not rely on. Lawsen (d16) shows part of the collapse is a token-limit and impossible-instance artefact.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: supports the regime picture (compute helps only in the middle) but is not a base rate for real agent work.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment on Shojaee et al.)
finding: Argues the 'accuracy collapse' is an experiment-design artefact. Tower of Hanoi runs exceed the output token limit and models say so. Some River Crossing instances (N of 6 or more) are mathematically impossible but were scored as failures. Asking for a generating function instead of a move list gave high accuracy on Hanoi sizes reported as complete failures.
numbers: Preliminary; no sample sizes or tables in the comment.
limits: Short comment with preliminary experiments; not a full replication.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: part of 'negative value of computation' on puzzles is output-budget truncation. A VOC gate must tell 'more thinking hurts' from 'ran out of budget'.

source: Ma, He, Snell, Griggs, Min, Zaharia (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking
finding: Re-check of weak spot c15. The 51.3 vs 28.9 number is confirmed in the abstract and results summary. Under a matched low token budget, skipping the thinking box beats thinking; with no budget limit thinking still wins at pass@1.
numbers: AMC23 with 700 tokens: NoThinking 51.3 vs Thinking 28.9. On theorem-proving sets NoThinking matches Thinking with 3.3-3.7x fewer tokens. NoThinking pass@k becomes competitive as k grows; parallel NoThinking with best-of-N is comparable to Thinking at up to 9x longer latency.
limits: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen only. Budget forcing cuts thinking off mid-way, so Thinking is penalised by truncation. In d10 NoThinking lost 12-17 average points on Qwen3-4B/8B.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the cheap gate 'skip thinking' is strong only at small budgets and is model-specific. It cannot be assumed for other model families.

source: Russell and Wefald (1991) Principles of Metareasoning, Artificial Intelligence 49 (access attempt)
finding: Not opened: ScienceDirect returned 403. Only the 1989 IJCAI and UAI predecessors (d01, d02) were read. Search confirmed the record as Artificial Intelligence vol. 49, 1991.
limits: Gap 7 stays open for the 1991 paper itself and for any modern replication.
agent_relevance: Do not cite specific 1991 numbers; cite the 1989 experiments with their limits.
